subject: physics
title: ECG, endoscopy and MRI
key_idea: An ECG records the tiny potential differences made by the beating heart. An endoscope uses total internal reflection in optical fibres to carry light and images. An MR scanner uses a strong magnetic field and radio pulses to make hydrogen nuclei emit signals that a computer turns into an image.

blocks.text: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is a record of the electrical activity of the heart. Heart muscle cells contract after a wave of electrical activity passes over them.

items.text: Electrodes on the skin, with conducting gel, pick up p.d.s of about 1 mV caused by the heart.
A differential amplifier with high gain boosts the small signal. It cancels interference that reaches both electrodes equally.
Filters remove unwanted frequencies, such as mains hum and signals from muscle movement.
The signal is shown as a trace of p.d. against time, on a screen or on paper.

blocks.text: Muscle cells become electrically active (depolarise) just before they contract, then reset (repolarise). The shape of the trace follows these events in order.

diagram.alt: An interactive ECG trace. Tap a feature to see what is happening in the heart.
diagram.prompt: Tap a part of the ECG waveform to see what it shows.

parts.name: P wave
parts.detail: A small peak. The atria depolarise, so the atria contract.

parts.name: PR segment
parts.detail: A flat part. The signal is delayed at the node between the atria and ventricles, so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start.

parts.name: QRS complex
parts.detail: A tall, narrow spike. The ventricles depolarise, so the ventricles contract. It is larger than the P wave because the ventricles have much more muscle.

parts.name: ST segment
parts.detail: A flat part. The ventricles are fully depolarised and still contracting.

parts.name: T wave
parts.detail: A broad, low peak. The ventricles repolarise and relax.

items: The atria repolarise at the same time as the QRS complex, but this signal is small and hidden by it.
The time between peaks gives the heart rate.
An abnormal shape, or irregular timing, can show a fault such as an irregular rhythm.
An ECG records the small p.d. at the skin made by the heart's electrical activity.
P wave: atria depolarise. QRS: ventricles depolarise. T wave: ventricles repolarise.
The QRS complex is the largest because the ventricles contain much more muscle than the atria.

blocks.text: An endoscope lets a doctor see inside the body through a small opening, using bundles of optical fibres. Each fibre carries light by total internal reflection.

items.meaning: The thin central strand of glass or plastic that carries the light.
The outer layer of glass with a lower refractive index than the core.
All the light is reflected back into the denser medium when it hits the boundary at an angle larger than the critical angle.

items: Light enters the core and hits the **core–cladding** boundary at an angle of incidence larger than the critical angle.
The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, so total internal reflection happens and no light is lost.
The light zigzags along the fibre, even when the fibre is bent.
The cladding protects the core from scratches, which would let light escape, and stops light leaking between neighbouring fibres.

blocks.label: Critical angle
where: n₁ = refractive index of the core
n₂ = refractive index of the cladding, which is smaller

rows: Fibres are in the same relative positions at both ends
Carrying the image back to the eyepiece or camera
Carrying light down to the tissue, which only needs light, not an image

items: Light goes down the non-coherent bundle to light up the inside of the body.
An objective lens at the tip forms a real image of the tissue on the end of the coherent bundle.
Each fibre carries the brightness of one small part of the image, so the image arrives intact at the other end.
A lens at the viewing end, or a camera, shows the image to the doctor.
Endoscopes can be inserted through the mouth or a very small cut, so no major surgery is needed.
The doctor sees the tissue directly in real time, and can take a sample (biopsy) or carry out a small operation with tools passed down a channel.
Recovery is quicker and there is less risk of infection than with open surgery.
Light stays in the core by total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary.
A coherent bundle carries the image. A non-coherent bundle carries illumination.
Endoscopy gives internal images with little damage to the patient.

blocks.text: A magnetic resonance (MR) scanner makes a cross-section image of the patient using magnetic fields and radio waves. It uses the hydrogen nuclei (protons) in water and fat.

items.meaning: A property of protons which makes each one behave like a tiny magnet.
The wobble of a spinning proton around the direction of a magnetic field.
Strong absorption of energy when the radio-wave frequency equals the precession frequency.

items.text: A superconducting magnet makes a strong, uniform field. Protons line up with their spins parallel to the field.
The protons precess about the field lines at a frequency which depends on the field strength.
Gradient coils make the field slightly stronger along the body, so protons in each slice precess at their own frequency.
A short radio frequency (RF) pulse at the precession frequency of one region excites the protons there. They change their spin state.
As the protons de-excite, they emit RF signals.
The RF signals are detected and a computer processes them to build up an image of the cross-section.

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the stages of an MR scan in the correct order.
diagram.prompt: Put the stages of an MR scan in order.
steps: Protons line up with their spins parallel to the strong magnetic field.
Gradient coils make the field vary so that each region has its own precession frequency.
A short RF pulse excites the protons in one small region.
The excited protons de-excite and emit RF signals.
A computer processes the detected signals to form an image.

items: Only the region whose precession frequency matches the pulse is excited, so the scanner scans small regions one after another.
The strength of the signal from a region depends on how many hydrogen nuclei are there, so tissues with different water content show up differently.
MR scanning does not use ionising radiation.
A strong field aligns the protons, and gradient coils make each region resonate at a different frequency.
RF pulses excite the protons, and the signals they emit as they de-excite are detected.
A computer turns the signals into a cross-section image.

checks.q: State why the QRS complex on an ECG is larger than the P wave.
checks.a: The QRS complex is the depolarisation of the ventricles, and the ventricles contain much more muscle than the atria, so the p.d. is larger.

checks.q: Explain how light travels along an optical fibre in an endoscope, and why the fibre has a cladding.
checks.a: Light hits the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected, and it zigzags along the core. The cladding has a lower refractive index than the core to make total internal reflection possible. It also protects the core from scratches and stops light passing between fibres.

checks.q: Describe the roles of the gradient coils and the RF pulses in an MR scanner.
checks.a: The gradient coils make the magnetic field vary across the patient, so protons in different small regions precess at different frequencies. A short RF pulse at one frequency excites only the protons in the matching region, and when they de-excite they emit RF signals that are detected.
